title_en: Ethics Watchdog Urges Investigation Into Top Health Official, Alleging Conflict of Interest Over Hormone Therapy Policy
excerpt_en: The post Ethics Watchdog Urges Investigation Into Top Health Official, Alleging Conflict of Interest Over Hormone Therapy Policy appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: The Campaign Legal Center is calling for an investigation into whether Alicia Jackson, director of the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, violated ethics laws. Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health A nonpartisan ethics watchdog group has asked for an investigation into whether a top Department of Health and Human Services official violated ethics laws after a recent ProPublica investigation revealed actions experts called “alarming” and an “obvious conflict of interest.”

Alicia Jackson, who heads the Advanced Research Projects Agency for Health, publicly endorsed a change to federal health policy on hormone replacement therapies while owning stock in a company that provides access to menopause treatments.

In a letter to the department’s inspector general, the Campaign Legal Center also questioned whether Jackson properly identified up to $400 million in underlying assets held by her husband’s investment firm. The center’s review identified an additional potential conflict — investments in a second firm that provides hormone treatments for menopause.
Jackson, who heads the HHS agency that invests taxpayer money in medical technology and research, was recently placed on administrative leave, though health officials have not publicly explained why.

In its letter, the Campaign Legal Center cited the ProPublica investigation that found Jackson spoke at an HHS press conference last November and was quoted in a department news release announcing the decision to remove “black box warnings” from hormone replacement therapy products.

At the time, Jackson owned at least $115,000 in stock and an unknown amount of stock options in Evernow, a company she founded that connects women to hormone replacement treatments, according to her financial disclosures.

Top U.S. Health Official Backed a Medication Policy Shift That Benefited a Company She Has Stock In It’s unclear what role, if any, Jackson played in the decision to drop the requirement to display a black box warning, the most serious type of federal safety warning. The Food and Drug Administration regulates drugs. And an FDA panel of experts had recommended ending the requirement months before Jackson became her agency’s director in October 2025.

Still, ethics experts noted that federal law prohibits government employees from participating “personally and substantially” in matters that could influence their personal finances — even making statements at a press conference or in a news release.

The Campaign Legal Center asked the inspector general to examine whether Jackson broke federal ethics laws by failing to recuse herself. Neither Jackson nor the HHS will say whether she obtained a conflict-of-interest waiver before participating in the policy announcement.
“Americans have a right to know that government decisions are not being made to benefit a federal employee’s financial interests,” the organization wrote.
The center also asked the inspector general to determine if Jackson failed to fully and accurately disclose her and her spouse’s financial interests in private investment funds.

ProPublica’s investigation found that Jackson reported she and her husband owned more than 60 venture capital and private equity funds that she said do not disclose their holdings to investors. These include at least 13 funds managed by 137 Ventures, a venture capital firm co-founded by her husband, Alex Jacobson. The company invests in a wide range of industries, including healthcare, digital health and medical device companies.
Ethics experts said the funds could pose a serious conflict of interest if the underlying businesses received grants or contracts from her agency.

137 Ventures founders Alex Jacobson, left, and Justin Fishner-Wolfson Kimberly White/Getty Images for 137 Ventures The Campaign Legal Center’s review of Jackson’s disclosures identified one of those funds — 137 Ventures IV LP — as an investor in Thirty Madison Inc., a virtual healthcare company. Thirty Madison owns a subsidiary that provides hormone replacement treatments for women experiencing menopause symptoms. Jackson’s disclosures do not show her divesting from the fund before the black box warning announcement, the center said.

Under federal law, financial disclosure forms filed by federal officials like Jackson must then be certified by ethics staff as complying with the law. But Jackson’s two financial disclosures — filed last October and two months ago — remain uncertified.

HHS’ inspector general’s office would not confirm or deny whether it is investigating Jackson. The inspector general, T. March Bell, was one of nearly 100 appointees confirmed by the Senate in a December 2025 party-line vote. President Donald Trump fired the previous inspector general just days into the president’s second term.

ProPublica also requested responses from HHS, Jackson, Jacobson and 137 Ventures, but none commented. In a statement to ProPublica last month, an HHS spokesperson said that while Jackson was on leave the agency would “assess the facts before determining any change in her status. HHS requires all officials to comply with federal ethics laws, regulations, and policies.”

Jackson was appointed by Trump as her agency’s second director and sworn in on Oct. 20, 2025. The agency, created three years earlier to spur revolutionary biomedical research and technologies, has a $1.5 billion budget. It has issued numerous contracts and grants, including $160 million for genetic medicines combating rare diseases and $144 million to study existing treatments for age-related illnesses.

Jackson’s disclosures are among 2,400 added last month to ProPublica’s Trump Team Financials database, a searchable tool launched in March. The records detail the finances of more than 2,300 officials appointed by Trump. Since last year, we’ve requested disclosure records from 127 federal agencies and the White House. Disclosures from roughly 1,500 appointees remain unreleased.

title_en: US flight outage live updates: FAA lifts nationwide ground stop; Trump officials suggest new tech overwhelmed old equipment
excerpt_en: Sean Duffy says ‘it’s going to take us some time to unwind what’s happened’ but also points finger at Congress, claiming lack of funding for systems upgrades
body_en: Ground stop lifts, but airport chaos and questions over US aviation system failure remain While the US Federal ⁠Aviation Administration has now lifted the nationwide ground stop imposed on airports just before 4pm Eastern Time, the question of what caused the communications outage that paralyzed the air-traffic control system remains to be answered.

On social media, Democrats on the House homeland security committee responded to comments from Markwayne Mullin, the head of homeland security, in which he seemed to suggest that patches to the system introduced by the FAA had caused the outage, by writing:

You brought the nation’s skies to a standstill. If you think Congressional Democrats will let you bury how this happened, you are sorely mistaken. Preserve all documents and emails. Oversight is coming.
As Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, acknowledged, the outage, which lasted more than 4 hours, had caused chaos and disruptions at airports that will take days to repair.
As those disruptions ripple through the global aviation system, we will continue to track the impact of Friday’s outage, and look for answers as to what, exactly, went wrong.

White House briefing filled with praise for Trump ends without clear explanation of what went wrong Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, and Markwayne Mullin, the head of homeland security, just concluded their briefing on the hours-long communications outage that led to chaos at US airports on Friday.

Both men peppered their remarks with lavish praise for Donald Trump, who was curiously quiet during the crisis that lasted for more than four hours. Neither of them offered a coherent explanation of what, exactly, had gone wrong – although they did seem to suggest that it was related to the installation of new technology in an antiquated system which caused older routers to be “overloaded with data” and fail.
“This is what the leadership of President Trump looks like,” Mullin began. “We’re built to handle crisis like this.”

Duffy then praised not just the president, but also his new chief of staff. “Stephen Miller put together all of the intelligence assets of the White House,” the former Fox News host and reality TV star said. “We were in multiple times talking to the president about what was happening in the airspace – complete engagement by President Trump’s team.”
“I want Congress to give us emergency funding,” Duffy said later. “I want $50bn. President Trump is a builder. He is going to build this network, and deliver for the American people.”
After one reporter asked why Trump was silent throughout the crisis, Mullin heaped still more praise on the president before calling the news conference to an end.

“I just can’t speak enough about President Trump’s leadership. This is what President Trump does: he puts leaders in place, and he allows them to lead,” Mullin said. “He’s the greatest president we’ve had, you’ve never had a builder and a leader like President Trump lead this nation, have a vision and put the put the team together. Thank you guys so much.”

Mullin appears to suggest older technology used by FAA was overwhelmed with data from new equipment Briefing reporters at the White House on Friday, Sean Duffy, the US transportation secretary, and Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, used the nationwide outage to press for more funding to overhaul the nation’s air-traffic-control system.

Both secretaries appeared to suggest that the cause of Friday’s outage was that older technology became overwhelmed with data after new technology was introduced. The FAA announced three days ago that a new air traffic management tool, known as Smart, was activated at all 22 air route traffic control centers in the US.

“The president for the last year has been asking Congress to fully fund a full build of a brand new air traffic control system,” Duffy said. “So we have TDM, telecom, so this is analog telecom. Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they went down and – I shouldn’t say they went down – they started to give us inconsistency in the data, from those, from those routers. And because of that, we shut the system down.”

“What it appears to be right now is”, Mullin said later, “as secretary Duffy and FAA was going in and putting patches into the system, they were putting new equipment and new technology and that new equipment, new technology just wasn’t- it was overwhelming the older system, which is why secretary Duffy made it very clear the patchwork doesn’t work. We need one complete system. We need someone to come in and build the whole system. Doing it- nickel and dime-ing it together does not work. This is what happens when that takes place. ”
Duffy denied the new Smart system, which incorporates artificial intelligence, had caused the problem.

'We have seen zero evidence that this was this was a cyber-attack,' Mullin says Markwayne Mullin, the US homeland security secretary, just told reporters at a briefing on the FAA outage that brought US aviation to a standpoint, “we’ve seen zero evidence that this was a cyber-attack.”

“Now, when we start looking at cyber threats, cyber-attacks, typically some people are going to raise their hand up and say, ‘hey, we did that. There’s no chatter. We haven’t seen any footprints, as you would say, or, identifications of people that got into the system,” Mullin added. “It appears that this was mechanically driven.”

title_en: SpaceX Starship megarocket blasts off before expected return for reuse
excerpt_en: Flight 15 expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over 22 hours, before company catches it at Starbase, Texas
body_en: SpaceX’s Starship megarocket blasted off from Texas on Friday afternoon as the aerospace company sought to make history with a double catch of its reusable rocket.

Starship, the world’s largest rocket, standing at 407ft, is expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over the course of 22 hours, before the company catches the rocket at its launchpad at Starbase in south Texas.
The rocket, which is on its 15th flight, is composed of two elements: the lower booster, with 33 raptor engines that fired off during takeoff, and the Starship at the top.
SpaceX had planned for both components to return to its tower, but the booster, named Super Heavy, was aborted, and splashed down in the sea. The cause of that diversion remains unknown.
The Starship, meanwhile, continued on sailing through space.

Friday’s test fell short of the double-catch mantle, but the flight is poised to mark another milestone for the company. If all goes to plan, it would be the first time SpaceX has caught the rocket’s 171ft upper stage.
Previous tests focused on the retrieval of the booster.
SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk has sought to advance Starship’s “rapid reusability”, which he hopes will take humans to the moon and, controversially, to Mars.
Nasa has contracted Space X, along with Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin, to provide the lunar landers that will return astronauts to the moon in 2028.
SpaceX has launched a flurry of test flights, in recent years, some of which have resulted in explosions that signaled major design flaws.
In September, the most recent flight test, SpaceX notched a victory, sending the spacecraft into Earth’s orbit for the first time, although its engine failed during the ascent.

title_en: Microsoft outage shakes up companies, schools and local governments across US
excerpt_en: Local officials warn some services remain unavailable even as Outlook starts to resume normal operations after outage
body_en: The Microsoft Outlook outage has shaken up companies and local governments across the US that use its suite of email, calendar, video conferencing and cloud storage systems.

Even as Outlook started to resume normal operations Friday morning, local leaders from across the country, including in Miami, Maryland and Los Angeles, warned residents that certain staff or services were still unavailable due to the outage that started around 1pm ET on Thursday.
In Colorado, one local detention facility in Arapahoe county said that they were unable to take online bond payments to release detainees because of the outage.
“Until Outlook email is restored, anyone needing to post bond for immediate release must do so in person at the jail,” the office said in a social media statement.
The Los Angeles county sheriff’s department also warned that it was experiencing disruptions in its email and other communications platforms.
Emergency management services in Fredericksburg and Gillespie county in Texas said they were unable to receive emails and encouraged residents and partners to call instead.

Around Maryland, the Washington suburban sanitary commission, which provides safe drinking water and sewer treatment to parts of Maryland, said that its technicians may be delayed due to the outage, and some customers may have trouble making their water bill payments.

In Washington DC, congressional staffers continued to lament the outage’s impact during the lame duck session of Congress. Some told Politico that the disruptions were particularly disruptive as their offices were in the middle of negotiating pending legislation before the end of the year and planning for the next Congress.
“Shall we start conducting all official business via DM?” wrote Sharon Eliza Nichols, the director of communications for congresswoman Eleanor Holmes Norton of Washington DC.

Some school districts in Richmond, Virginia, and Port Washington, New York, also told parents on Friday morning that they were experiencing outages, and asked them to reach out by phone or through other online educational platforms to reach their child’s school, while the Albany school district said that it had restored its services.

The Colorado School of Mines encouraged “faculty to be flexible with assignment deadlines and understanding of students who cannot complete assignments due to unavailability of Microsoft tools”, though many of its systems were on unaffected platforms such as Google Workspace and Canvas.

Claude, whose developer, Anthropic, is gearing up for its upcoming stock market debut with a valuation of up to $1.4tn, also said that it was starting to see signs of recovery from the Microsoft outages, but warned that some users may still receive errors. OpenAI also said it was still investigating issues with “Microsoft connectors” that were degrading performance.
“We’re investigating an issue with Microsoft connectors where new connections may be broken and tools are not working as expected. We’ll share an update when we know more,” the company said.
On Wall Street, Workhorse Group, an industrial manufacturer, rescheduled its Q3 earnings call that was scheduled for Thursday afternoon because of the outage.
In a social media post, Microsoft executive Charles Lamanna said late Thursday that “there is no indication this is the result of malicious or cyber activity”.

On Friday morning, Microsoft noted “improvements in service availability” but noted that “some users may still experience intermittent access issues or delayed email delivery as a recovery continues”.

By the end of the day, most of the issues seemed to be ironed out. Schools and businesses appeared to be coming back online, congressional staffers reported “improvements to Outlook’s functionality”. The Colorado detention facility said it is “now receiving email notifications when online bond payments are made”.
And the emergency management services in Texas said they were starting to see emails trickle back in, saying: “Thanks for your patience with the worldwide outage!”
Dara Kerr and Johana Bhuiyan contributed reporting

title_en: Could you survive without Microsoft? Inside the costs of digital dependence
excerpt_en: Digital choices have huge environmental costs but these are rarely counted up.
body_en: Microsoft products including Outlook were out of action globally on November 13 2026. Alex Photo Stock/Shutterstock When I arrived at work to discover that Outlook had vanished from my computer, I wondered how I was supposed to get through my working day. No emails. No calendar. No meeting invitations.

Then another thought crossed my mind: when did we become so dependent on a single technology company that losing access to one application could disrupt our entire working routine? And what is the financial and environmental cost of that dependence?

We regularly discuss sustainability in terms of reducing plastic, cutting carbon emissions and consuming less energy. But the digital systems we rely on every day also have huge environmental consequences.

As world leaders gather at the UN climate summit, Cop31, in Turkey, perhaps it is time to ask an uncomfortable question: can our digital economy really become sustainable when so much of it depends on a handful of technology companies?
The cloud has a physical footprint The cloud may sound weightless, but it runs on data centres, electricity, cooling systems and hardware.

The International Energy Agency estimates that data centres consumed 415 terawatt-hours of electricity in 2024, around 1.5% of global demand. It projects that consumption could reach 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, largely driven by AI and other digital services.

Microsoft’s own 2026 sustainability report illustrates the tension. The company reported a 25% year-over-year rise in total emissions in 2025, primarily because of expanding data centres and a change in renewable-energy certificate accounting. Microsoft is also investing in cleaner energy and more efficient infrastructure. Both facts matter: technological progress can reduce emissions per task, while growth pushes overall demand higher.

Asking the right questions Turkey’s Cop31 presidency released the voluntary Antalya artificial intelligence pledge in October. This pledge aims to encourage climate-responsible AI while acknowledging the energy and water demands of the technology.

The World Resources Institute, a global research organisation, welcomed the pledge’s direction but warned that voluntary commitments need stronger accountability mechanisms. Meanwhile, the International Telecommunication Union has scheduled a Cop31 event for November 16 on financing cleaner digital infrastructure, measuring emissions, and promoting durable, repairable and reusable electronics.

The message is important: sustainability cannot stop at greener electricity. It also concerns what technology organisations purchase, how long they keep it, and who pays for its environmental effects.

When a software decision becomes a hardware bill Consider a computer that still works but cannot support a newer operating system. Windows 10’s regular support ended in October 2025, although Microsoft offers extended security updates for eligible consumer devices through October 2027.
The transition does not make every older computer obsolete. Yet software support and compatibility can influence whether organisations replace otherwise usable equipment.

Manufacturing devices consumes energy and raw materials. It also creates electronic waste (e-waste). According to the UN’s global e-waste monitor, the world generated 62 million metric tonnes of e-waste in 2022, of which just 22.3% was documented as formally collected and recycled.
These figures cover all electronic waste, not waste attributable to Microsoft. They nevertheless show why extending equipment lifetimes deserves a place in climate policy.

What are the environmental costs of using data and digital? Costs that are rarely counted A software subscription has a visible price. Less visible are the costs of training employees, migrating files, replacing equipment, maintaining duplicate systems and eventually switching suppliers.
Economists call these switching costs. They can lock organisations into existing providers even when better-value alternatives emerge.

This is not merely hypothetical. In March 2026, the UK’s Competition and Markets Authority announced plans to investigate Microsoft’s business software ecosystem. It also reported steps by major cloud service providers, including Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services, to reduce data-transfer fees and improve interoperability, making it easier for businesses to switch between providers.

What might this have to do with sustainability? A buyer unable to change providers easily may also struggle to choose lower-emission computing services. That is a potential environmental consequence of lock-in, not a demonstrated claim that Microsoft users emit more carbon.

There is a wider accounting problem too. The UN estimates that global electronic waste was associated with approximately US$78 billion (£59 billion) in externalised costs in 2022, including pollution and climate-related impacts. Such costs are largely absent from the price of a software license.
A responsible procurement decision should therefore compare lifetime financial costs, equipment lifespans and credible emissions data rather than only the next annual bill.

Freedom to choose Could workplaces use alternatives (such as Thunderbird and LibreOffice) or interoperable cloud services? Often, yes. But migration has costs and a rival provider is not necessarily greener.
The better goal is freedom to choose: portable data, open document formats, repairable devices, transparent environmental reporting and software contracts that do not penalise switching.

title_en: Members of Georgia’s Election Board Have Been Coordinating With Cleta Mitchell’s Network
excerpt_en: The post Members of Georgia’s Election Board Have Been Coordinating With Cleta Mitchell’s Network appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: The Georgia State Election Board meets in Marietta in March. Mauricio Rodriguez Pons/ProPublica In the run-up to the midterms, members of Georgia’s State Election Board and much of its professional staff were coordinating with an activist group led by Cleta Mitchell, the conservative attorney who worked with President Donald Trump to try to overturn his defeat in the 2020 election.
The board sets the swing state’s election rules, oversees the conduct of its election officials and investigates allegations of fraud.

Recordings of private calls and events reviewed by ProPublica show current and former state board members working with the Election Integrity Network and allied organizations on shared priorities. Among them: advancing the use of a controversial, error-prone software tool known as ELLY to search voter rolls for purportedly suspicious voters.

The state board’s current vice chair, Janelle King, and her predecessor, Janice Johnston, have both attended meetings of EIN or VoterGA, an aligned organization whose membership and goals significantly overlap with EIN. Johnston retired in June but still plays an active role in state election matters behind the scenes.
At an August 2025 fundraiser for VoterGA, Mitchell declared she loved Johnston and King, who were both present. “You know, we’ve worked so hard together,” Mitchell said.

Janice Johnston and Janelle King at a March meeting of the State Election Board. Johnston resigned from the board in June. Mauricio Rodriguez Pons/ProPublica At least three members of the state board’s eight-person professional staff have participated in EIN meetings, including people who handle allegations of voter fraud and misconduct by election officials.

The board’s executive director, James Mills, likewise has worked closely with members of the EIN, according to five sources with knowledge of these interactions, board documents and EIN communications shared with ProPublica.

EIN’s close ties to the board and its staff have given it extraordinary influence over how elections are run in Georgia, experts said. In particular, the group has been able to enlist the board’s help in getting counties to remove voters from their rolls based on information from ELLY.

“Trump allies captured the State Election Board to keep claims of a stolen 2020 election going and tilt Georgia elections toward Republicans,” said Max Flugrath, a director at Fair Fight Action, a voting advocacy nonprofit that has closely tracked the board’s and the network’s actions. “EIN was the behind-the-scenes driver spearheading these changes.”
The board’s chair, John Fervier, told ProPublica he had not known about EIN’s sway over the board or its staff, but said he’d long sensed that an outside force was shaping the board’s actions.

“The more I look into this, the more I’m realizing that the Election Integrity Network has been having an undue influence on the State Election Board, and that needs to cease,” he said in an interview, though he declined to go into specifics about personnel matters. “I’m looking forward to changes in how the election board operates.”
John Fervier has chaired the Georgia State Election Board since 2024. Mauricio Rodriguez Pons/ProPublica Fervier has called a special meeting for Friday, in part to discuss personnel matters.

In response, Garland Favorito, an EIN leader and head of VoterGA, called on social media for his followers to inundate state board members with messages defending Mills and other staffers associated with the group.

“There is a significant possibility that these members will vote to terminate the Executive Director, investigators or possibly even staff members, any of which would destroy the SEB as we now know it,” Favorito wrote on Wednesday, referring to the State Election Board. “As most of you know, the SEB staff has made remarkable historical progress this year in … accountability for election corruption and much more. The Executive Director and staff deserve raises for amazing performances, not threats of termination.”

In interviews in late September, Johnston did not directly answer questions about her relationship to EIN. “I’m all about election integrity, wherever it comes from,” she said. She acknowledged she had remained involved with board affairs after her retirement. “It gets in your blood,” she said. Two days later, she posted on social media that “Cleta Mitchell, Election Integrity expert has the right ideas” about how elections should be run.
Johnston did not answer detailed questions about her relationship with EIN and affiliated groups.

King was appointed to the board by the Republican-led Georgia House in 2024. Mauricio Rodriguez Pons/ProPublica King acknowledged she spoke about election matters with activists from EIN and VoterGA, but said they did not influence her decisions. She also said she saw no problem with EIN activists working for the board, though the staff is supposed to be independent and nonpartisan.
“As long as they are representing the SEB well, fine,” she said in an interview. “If they choose to become members of an organization in their private time, that is their choice.”

When a reporter recounted instances in which staffers had worked to advance EIN goals in their official capacity, she said she was unaware of this. “That is the first I’ve heard about it,” she responded.
Mills declined to answer questions from ProPublica about his relationship to EIN.

Mitchell did not respond directly to ProPublica but, after receiving detailed questions, put a post on X celebrating EIN’s work with the election board. “An election integrity group is working with election officials to oversee elections,” she wrote. “Wow! What a discovery!!! Pulitzer anyone?”
Favorito called the idea that the board and its staff had been working secretly with the EIN and VoterGA a “patently false conspiracy theory.”

title_en: His Church or His Child? A Sixth-Generation Member of a Faith-Healing Sect Had to Choose.
excerpt_en: The post His Church or His Child? A Sixth-Generation Member of a Faith-Healing Sect Had to Choose. appeared first on ProPublica.
body_en: Photo illustration: Mauricio Rodríguez Pons/ProPublica. Source images: Beth Nakamura/The Oregonian, courtesy of the Phillips family. What if you had to pick between your deeply held faith and the life of your child? That’s the gutting choice that faced Marshall Phillips, an Oregon dad who was born into the Followers of Christ, a sect whose creed bars medical treatment. When his 11-year-old son was stricken with a dire health crisis, Phillips became caught between his faith, his family and the state of Oregon, which had begun cracking down on faith-healing parents who don’t seek medical help for their minor children. A decade later, Phillips was pulled into another one of his church’s life-or-death dramas when he was asked to care for a newborn whose twin had died because her parents had refused to seek medical attention.

Prophecy, Scorn and a Rejection of This World: The Forbidding Vision of a Faith-Healing Preacher To examine the power of faith-healing churches and the toll of their teachings, The Oregonian investigative reporter Noelle Crombie, senior staff photojournalist Beth Nakamura and videographer Samantha Swindler spent months with Phillips and his family, piecing together rare accounts from inside the deeply shuttered world of the Followers of Christ and of the state officials who fought to protect children who need medical treatment. The documentary, produced by The Oregonian’s managing producer of video, Teresa Mahoney, not only lays out in visceral detail the agonizing choices that families like the Phillips have to make, it also chronicles how they overcame the clash with their religious beliefs.
Go inside the secretive Followers of Christ sect and watch the extraordinary journey. Read more in this riveting print narrative, and meet the man who dominated and shaped the sect.

title_en: Young turtles find refuge in both natural and artificial wetlands in UAE – new study
excerpt_en: A large basin was never used for its intended recreational purposes and has since been incorporated into a marine protected area alongside coastal mangroves.
body_en: Coastal wetlands, such as mangroves and saltmarshes, are rapidly disappearing yet they are incredibly important for young turtles.

In a new study, my colleagues and I used satellite tags to track young green turtles in a protected wetland in Sharjah, UAE. Our results reveal just how important these remaining natural spaces are to young turtles.

But we also found that nature can find a way to thrive in unexpected, human-made environments too. So protecting these habitats and the connections between wetlands, artificial environments and the open sea is essential to ensuring wildlife can persist in an increasingly human-shaped world.

Coastal wetlands protect our shorelines from storms, store carbon and provide important nursery habitats for marine life. Yet scientists still know surprisingly little about how marine wildlife, including turtles, sharks and rays, use these environments. Knowing where these animals feed, shelter and move helps identify which areas need protection and whether existing protected areas are working.

Our study, a collaborative effort between the Environment and Protected Areas Authority (EPAA), a UAE government agency, the University of Exeter and the Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre, focused on Al Qurm Wa Lehhfaiiah, a marine protected area encompassing the last major coastal wetland ecosystem on the UAE’s east coast, which is called Khor Kalba.

Its complex wetlands support migratory wading birds, numerous fish species and the Arabian collared kingfisher, a subspecies found only in this region. Young green turtles also swim through its winding mangrove channels.

Although the wetland is now protected and recognised as a Ramsar site, a type of conservation designation for any internationally important wetlands, it has not escaped human development. The city of Kalba surrounds much of the site, and a large human-made basin (like a lagoon) was built alongside the natural mangroves in the early 2000s as a proposed recreational and commercial waterfront. The basin was never used for its intended recreational purposes and has since been incorporated into the protected area.

To understand how young turtles use this unusual landscape alongside the natural mangrove channels, EPAA staff carefully captured nine juvenile green turtles in 2019 and attached satellite tags to their shells using a specialist, harmless resin. After the turtles were released, the tags allowed us to follow their movements.

After seven months and over 2,800 satellite locations the results were clear. We found Kalba’s wetlands were a critical habitat for all nine turtles. They generally stayed within just 2 miles of the wetland entrance and spent more than 80% of their tracked time inside the marine protected area’s boundary.

Basin benefits One of the more surprising findings was the popularity of the human-made basin (similar to a saltwater lagoon extending from the mangroves). The turtles were around five times more likely to be found there than elsewhere in the wetland, and 77% of their core-use areas were concentrated within it.

We cannot say for certain why the turtles favoured the basin. One possibility is that algae growing on its floor provides food, while its enclosed layout may offer shelter from larger predators. Whatever the explanation, the findings suggest that wildlife can make use of human-modified environments.

However, this is no substitute for protecting natural habitats. Where coastal environments are modified or restored, designs that retain natural habitats, maintain connections between them and preserve the ecological processes they depend on may offer the greatest benefits for wildlife.

One turtle eventually embarked on a very different journey. After remaining in the wetland for 93 days, it travelled over 500 miles to Masirah Island in neighbouring Oman. This remarkable journey highlights how a small coastal wetland can be important to young turtles before they move into wider waters.

But the study also revealed a gap in protection. The main natural channel connecting the ocean to the mangroves and basin currently lies outside the marine protected area. Although the turtles used this channel less frequently overall, they gathered there at low tide, possibly waiting for rising water to allow them to move back into the wetland. Extending protection to include this connecting channel could therefore strengthen the conservation value of the entire system.

Our findings underline the importance of protecting natural coastal wetlands. The human-made basin may offer unexpected benefits, but the natural mangrove channels and their connection to the sea remain essential parts of the wider ecosystem.

As coastal development continues around the world, understanding how wildlife uses both natural and modified environments can help us make better conservation decisions. Protecting the remaining wetlands at Kalba, including the connections between them and the ocean, is an important step towards securing a future for the young turtles that depend on them.
Owen Exeter receives funding from the Environment and Protected Areas Authority (EPAA), the University of Exeter and the Sharjah Marine Science Research Centre.

title_en: Anthony Albanese’s coffee diplomacy can’t remove shadow of domestic politics at Cop31
excerpt_en: The Australian prime minister’s use of traditional skills – and free flat whites – brought success in Turkey. But his country’s fossil fuel industry and its culture wars remain a problem
body_en: Being cynical comes easy at a UN climate summit, but there was a faint glimmer of something else on the face of the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese. Pride.

Standing to face journalists at his only press conference here at Cop31 in Antalya on Thursday, Albanese was flanked by seven leaders from the Pacific. He said he was privileged to be standing with them and proud of what Australia was doing to help them access funding to deal with the climate crisis.
Related: ‘Start listening’: Indigenous activist implores Albanese to block new coal, oil and gas

Politicians say this kind of thing all the time, but this felt believable. Albanese was beaming. Colloquially known as Albo, he flew into Cop31 on Wednesday morning as one of more than 90,000 delegates to visit this UN and flew out on Friday afternoon.

With his climate change minister, Chris Bowen, in the position of president of negotiations, Albanese became a significant figure in the talks, speaking at high-level meetings over a two-and-a-half day visit that was a perfect encapsulation of the contradictions that, for now, have to exist together in climate diplomacy.

That contradiction is that a country like Australia can advocate for climate action while still being a major fossil fuel producer. The problems came when Albanese failed to name the central problem – fossil fuels.

His big public moment came only a few hours after stepping off the plane with a travelling press pack and a ready handshake for the Turkish president, Recep Erdoğan, and the UN secretary general, António Guterres.
Related: More than 100 companies and groups linked to fossil fuels represented at Cop31, study says

In the vast plenary hall here, Guterres was typically bold in the conference opening, saying as heat records were being shattered, “fossil fuel interests keep making a killing … while killing our planet”.
But then came the perfectly timed kicker, saying developed countries “cannot keep expanding fossil fuel production while claiming to be committed to 1.5 degrees”.

Perfectly timed because Albanese was next on stage – the leader of one such developed country that is the second largest exporter of thermal coal, the largest exporter of coal for steelmaking and that is also responsible for a fifth of seaborne LNG.
This was the “critical decade” Albanese said, and he was “proud to be a leader on climate action”.

A report released by the research organisations Germanwatch and New Climate Institute disagreed. For its policies and efforts to mitigate climate change, Australia was ranked as a “very low” performer.
Australia has promised to raise the plight of its Pacific neighbours at this Cop, and Albanese Bowen have done it regularly in speeches and statements.

During his address, Albanese read a message from 13-year-old Melelusi Sokotia, a student in the low-lying Pacific nation of Tuvalu, who told a pre-Cop meeting that she had a “simple dream” to grow up safely on the island.
Albanese said Australia was “proud to be here fighting for the interests of our Pacific family” and island nations in that region were “pleading for us” to take action.

‘One of the most important events I’ve ever been to’ But action on what? As Guterres had said, the answer was to move away from producing and burning fossil fuels, but the f-words never left Albanese’s lips. It was an awkward omission that Albanese later defended by saying you could “pick out any number of things that weren’t in what was a short speech”.

Perhaps the refusal to name the heart of the problem is down to the political landscape in Australia, where a climate science-denying far-right populist party, One Nation, is level in the polls with Albanese’s Labor, and the official opposition centre-right Liberal party wants to scrap net zero climate goals.

Although it is a challenge faced by leaders of all developed nations, Albanese’s dilemma is particularly acute. “I think the PM has to walk a fine line between the domestic politics of climate change that’s getting harder, and the urgent need for strong action,” Matt Kean, the chair of Australia’s Climate Change Authority, told the Guardian. “And he is doing it successfully.”
Kean should know. He was a treasurer and energy minister in the Liberal government of New South Wales, and has been at the sharp end of the politics of climate change.

He said Albanese’s successes included hosting abreakfast that brought together major investors, including a large Canadian pension fund, a Japanese investment bank and other multi-billion dollar organisations, and Australian renewable energy companies.

“It was one of the most consequential and important events I’ve ever been to at these conferences,” said Kean. “Australia gathered in a room some of the biggest capital allocators in the world with Australian renewables developers … I think it was incredibly impactful.”

title_en: Jimmy Kimmel on Trump accusing Democrats of wrongdoing: ‘His mantra is corruption’
excerpt_en: Late-night hosts poked fun at the president taking JD Vance off Iran duty to sniff out corruption while expressing annoyance at Democrats for failing to impeach Pete Hegseth
body_en: Late-night hosts ridiculed Donald Trump ’s latest efforts to accuse Democrats of corruption while showing frustration over democratic behavior this week.
Jimmy Kimmel On Jimmy Kimmel Live!, the host started by reminding his viewers that with the latest historic victory in Mississippi, the Democrats now have 55 seats in the Senate and 255 in the House.
Related: Seth Meyers on Trump’s midterms denial: ‘Watching you go through the motions is bumming me out’

It’s taken Trump “a week to digest that massive defeat” and now he has hopped “onboard the bipolar express” to accuse Democrats of corruption and claim that he is the first president not to accept a salary, which is false.
Kimmel also noted that there’s only proof of him turning down his very first presidential paycheck and suggested that the following payments might have been applied to the ballroom.

Trump also suggested that “the caravans are back” despite his earlier warnings never leading to a mass arrival in the first place. “I guess those guys got lost in Tijuana for a few years,” Kimmel said.
The host said that Trump is “shrieking” but that “nobody’s listening”.
This week also saw the president make JD Vance the lead Iran negotiator before he “pulled the plug” and instead had him root out alleged corruption and crime in Democratic-run cities and states.
Kimmel speculated that he didn’t want Vance getting credit for ending the war, which would be his “nightmare”, and called the new job “so ridiculous for so many reasons”.
He joked that “Trump telling you to root out corruption is like Colonel Sanders telling you to root out cholesterol”.
Kimmel said that instead “his mantra is corruption” and that Vance “almost had a real job to do, he was so close”.
One of the week’s biggest stories has been the “tech-sex scandal” involving Nvidia’s Jenson Huang, who allegedly had an affair with two women including a Chinese spy.
Trump called him an “honorable man” yet Kimmel suggested that “his wife called him something else”.

The president was informed of the situation as early as October last year but has “dodged that allegation a few times”, and while Huang is “supposed to be a genius” there have now been “a lot of photos” surfacing of the pair in public.
Kimmel called them “a couple of Nvidiots”.
Seth Meyers On Late Night, Seth Meyers also spoke about the midterm elections and replayed footage of Republicans who “kept insisting the polls were wrong” before the blue wave took place.
But Meyers added that “the results that came after the election were even crazier”, including this week in Mississippi, where Democrat Scott Colom became the first Black senator since Reconstruction.
Meyers called it “payback” given that Colom had previously been blocked from being appointed to a federal judgeship by his Republican rival, Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Meyers said it was “a beautiful story of revenge” and that it “sounds like something George would do in an episode of Seinfeld”.
He also noted that polling shows Pete Hegseth to be less popular than Trump, which means the president will keep him “around so he looks good in comparison”.
He played a montage of Hegseth saying variously vile things, including a viral list of the types he doesn’t want in the military. “Did you think people were gonna love your incel poetry?” he asked.
This week saw an impeachment attempt by Thomas Massie, whom Meyers called “a sassy Republican”, yet a number of Democrats just didn’t make the vote, leading to a frustrating lack of support.

title_en: Microsoft has suffered a global outage. A tech expert explains what went wrong
excerpt_en: This outage shows why we must urgently prepare for digital outages in a similar way we do for natural disasters.
body_en: Angel Bena/Pexels Microsoft has suffered a major global outage, bringing many of its widely used tools, including email and cloud storage, to a standstill.

According to outage tracking site DownDetector, some 130,000 people reported issues accessing Microsoft Outlook as of early Thursday afternoon US Eastern time (early Friday morning in Sydney). In a statement on X, the tech giant said it was “aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact” and “restarting affected servers to return them to service”.
In an article for The Conversation last month, I explained how the whole internet is unlikely to go down but several services can become unavailable together when they rely on shared systems.
This outage shows precisely what happens when that shared infrastructure fails – and why we must prepare for digital outages in a similar way we do for natural disasters.

Beyond missed emails or workplace meetings The list of services Microsoft says are “potentially impacted” by the outage is long. It includes services used for email, document sharing, meetings and managing tasks, such as Outlook, Microsoft Teams, SharePoint Online, Microsoft Copilot 365, Microsoft Planner and Microsoft Exchange Online. It also includes Microsoft Defender, a cloud-based cybersecurity service.
With so many digital services affected, the real-world impacts of the outage have been widespread, and go far beyond missed emails or workplace meetings.

For example, family violence workers reportedly can’t access databases which contain client details. Schools can’t provide online lessons for remote students. Psychologists can’t provide telehealth consultations. Businesses are unable to process orders. Job hunters are unable to make it to planned interviews. Some government service centres have been forced to closed.
The disruption also reached services outside Microsoft. OpenAI and Anthropic reported problems with the tools that connect their artificial intelligence (AI) services to Microsoft 365.
This shows how a problem in one part of the digital world can affect tools that appear separate, and even services provided by other companies.

The outage comes after other disruptions to Microsoft services earlier this year. For example, in January, Outlook, Teams and other Microsoft 365 services were down for hours. Then in August, Microsoft Outlook and Exchange Online were disrupted by a code update which took several days to fix.

A shifting account of what went wrong As of early Friday afternoon Sydney time, Microsoft has not yet named a root cause of the outage, and its account of the failure has shifted since it was first reported.

Initially the company said elevated load across multiple regions was reported first. It then clarified the load was not driven by an increase in traffic, but a large number of servers becoming unexpectedly unavailable.
Attention then moved to the automated “health checks” Microsoft uses to judge whether a server is fit to carry traffic, and to the component that processes them.

The company described a core process on the affected servers as becoming “overwhelmed”. Software deployments and configuration changes were paused while recent changes were reviewed, although none was found to correlate with the start of the disruption.
The evidence does not suggest a cyberattack.

A distributed denial-of-service attack works by flooding a service with requests from outside until legitimate ones can no longer be answered. Microsoft’s own statement that overall traffic had not increased is difficult to reconcile with that pattern. No evidence of malicious activity has been disclosed, and no group has claimed responsibility.
Indeed, Microsoft said: “There’s no indication this is a cyber attack.”

The more mundane explanation fits better. Health checks exist to protect a service by withdrawing servers that appear unwell. When the machinery making that judgement is itself at fault, healthy capacity can be removed, and the servers that remain are left to absorb work they were never sized for.
Outages of this scale are more often self-inflicted in this way than they are the work of attackers, as the August disruption to Microsoft email by a code update illustrates.
Until a post-incident review is published, however, that remains an inference drawn from Microsoft’s own updates rather than a settled account.
Microsoft has not yet been able to fix the outage entirely. It says that some of the affected servers are working again, but they “can become unresponsive again once they begin receiving traffic”.

Planning for outages like we do for bushfires This outage reinforces the need for all of us to better prepare for digital outages. For individuals, this can involve storing essential information, such as contacts and medical prescriptions, offline in case of an outage.
